steps.margin_note: The key word is DIRECTION — the conserved direction of L is what resists tilting.
steps.why: Angular momentum is a vector. Tilting the bicycle would change the direction of L, and that needs a torque — so small disturbances fail to tip it. This is the board answer. In full detail a rider also balances by steering the wheels back under the centre of mass; write the angular-momentum reason in the exam.
common_mistakes: Saying only "because of speed". Speed alone balances nothing; the spinning wheels do.

recall.must_convey: That the spinning wheels have angular momentum whose direction is conserved.

steps.margin_note: Close the loop: conserved direction → tilting needs torque → small pushes fail → balance.
steps.why: A stationary bicycle has no angular momentum to protect it — any small lean grows. Motion gives the wheels a stored direction that fights the lean.
common_mistakes: Stopping at "angular momentum is conserved" without connecting it to not tipping.

recall.must_convey: That tilting needs a torque the disturbances cannot supply, so the bicycle stays balanced.
